title: Move Out Cleaning Checklist: Room by Room to Protect Your Deposit
seo_title: Move Out Cleaning Checklist: Room-by-Room Guide
meta_description: A room-by-room move out cleaning checklist for the kitchen, bathrooms, floors and walls, plus the spots landlords check and what to use.
body_html:
Move-out cleaning is the last thing standing between you and your security deposit, and it always takes longer than you think. The trick is to clean in the right order, hit the spots landlords actually inspect, and leave yourself time to fix what you miss. Use this room-by-room checklist to get it done in one organized push.

Before you start: plan your timing

Clean after the furniture and boxes are out, not before. Empty rooms are faster to clean and you will spot things that were hidden behind the couch or under the bed.

  • Block out a full day for a one-bedroom, more for a larger place. Ovens and bathrooms take the longest.
  • Reread your lease for cleaning requirements. Some leases require professional carpet cleaning or specify a cleaning fee.
  • Pull out your move-in photos and inspection form so you know what condition the unit started in.
  • Keep the power and water on until you finish. You need lights, hot water, and outlets for the vacuum.

If you have roommates, split the work by room and agree on who checks whose area at the end. A second pair of eyes catches things you stop noticing after a few hours of scrubbing.

If you are moving across the country, fit this into your bigger timeline with our long distance apartment move checklist.

Gather your supplies

Having everything in one bucket saves a lot of trips. A basic kit:

  • All-purpose cleaner, glass cleaner, degreaser, and bathroom cleaner
  • Microfiber cloths, scrub brushes, a grout brush, and non-scratch sponges
  • Melamine foam sponges for wall scuffs
  • Vacuum with attachments, broom, dustpan, and mop
  • Trash bags, rubber gloves, and a step stool
  • Spackle and a putty knife for small nail holes, if your lease allows patching

Always follow the label directions, test cleaners on a hidden spot first, and never mix bleach with ammonia or other cleaners.

Work top to bottom, back to front

In every room, clean from high to low: ceiling fans and light fixtures first, then walls and counters, then floors last. Dust falls down, so cleaning floors first means doing them twice. Start with the room farthest from the front door and work your way out, so you are not walking through spaces you already finished.

Kitchen checklist

The kitchen is usually the first place a landlord looks, and grease is the most common complaint.

  • Oven: remove racks, clean the interior, racks, door glass, and the drawer underneath. Self-cleaning ovens need ventilation and time, so start early.
  • Stovetop: degrease burners, drip pans, knobs, and the area under a lift-up cooktop.
  • Range hood: wipe the hood and soak or clean the filter.
  • Refrigerator: empty it completely, remove and wash shelves and drawers, wipe the gaskets, and clean the outside and top. Pull it out if you can and sweep behind it.
  • Microwave and dishwasher: wipe the interior, clean the dishwasher filter, and wipe door edges.
  • Cabinets and drawers: empty, vacuum crumbs, wipe inside and out, and remove any shelf liner you added.
  • Sink and counters: scrub the sink, polish the faucet, and wipe the backsplash.

Bathroom checklist

  • Tub and shower: scrub soap scum, grout, and the shower door or curtain rod. Clear hair from the drain.
  • Toilet: clean the bowl, seat, hinges, base, and the floor around it.
  • Sink and vanity: scrub the sink, polish fixtures, and wipe inside drawers and the cabinet.
  • Mirror and medicine cabinet: glass cleaner on the mirror, empty and wipe shelves.
  • Exhaust fan: dust the cover. Turn off power first if you remove it.
  • Floors: mop, paying attention to corners and behind the toilet.

Bedrooms, living areas, and closets

  • Dust ceiling fans, light fixtures, vents, and the tops of door frames.
  • Wipe light switches, outlet covers, doorknobs, and doors.
  • Gently remove scuffs from walls. Test first, since scrubbing can remove paint.
  • Remove nails, hooks, and adhesive strips carefully. Patch small holes if your lease permits it.
  • Wipe window sills, tracks, and blinds. Clean the inside of windows.
  • Empty closets fully, wipe the shelves, and vacuum the floor.
  • Wipe baseboards last before vacuuming.

Floors, extras, and the spots people forget

Finish with floors, then sweep through the extras. These are the places that get missed in a rush:

  • Inside the washer and dryer, plus the lint trap and the floor behind them
  • Patio or balcony, storage closets, garage, and mailbox
  • Air vents and returns; replace the HVAC filter if your lease makes that your job
  • Light bulbs that burned out, if replacing them is your responsibility
  • Smoke alarms that are chirping or missing batteries
  • Every last item, including food in the pantry and trash in outdoor bins

Vacuum carpets thoroughly, including edges with a crevice tool. Sweep and mop hard floors. If your lease requires professional carpet cleaning, keep the receipt.

Quick reference: what to focus on

AreaMost important tasksEasy to forget
KitchenOven, stovetop, fridge interiorRange hood filter, under the stove drawer
BathroomTub grout, toilet, sinkExhaust fan cover, drains
Living areasWall scuffs, floorsTops of door frames, outlet covers
Closets and storageEmpty fullyGarage, patio, storage units

Finish with photos and a walkthrough

When you are done, take a full set of photos and a walkthrough video, ideally in the same order as your move-in photos. Open the oven, fridge, and cabinets on camera. Keep a small kit of supplies in your car until after the walkthrough, so you can fix a missed spot on the spot instead of paying a cleaning charge. Ask your landlord for a final walkthrough, return all keys, and give your forwarding address in writing. For the full process, read our guide on how to get your security deposit back.

Deposit rules vary by state, and this is not legal advice. In Texas, a landlord generally must refund the deposit or provide an itemized list of deductions within 30 days after you surrender the unit, and cannot charge for normal wear and tear.

Frequently asked questions

Should I hire a professional move-out cleaner?

It can be worth it if you are short on time or the unit needs deep cleaning. Ask for a receipt and take your own photos afterward to confirm the result.

Do I need to clean the carpets?

Check your lease. Some require professional carpet cleaning at move-out; others only expect a thorough vacuum. Normal wear in traffic areas generally should not be charged.

Should I paint before moving out?

Usually not without asking. A mismatched touch-up can look worse than a scuff. If you painted a different color, ask the landlord what they expect.

How long does move-out cleaning take?

For many one-bedroom units it takes most of a day, longer if the oven or bathroom needs deep cleaning. Start earlier than you think you need to.
